title: Magha Puja, the fifth time
hookLine: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind
tomorrow: the Buddha found his way by remembering one afternoon. which one?

lines: THE BAMBOO GROVE, A FULL MOON.
cards: Someone volunteers every Saturday, gives to every fundraiser, never misses a birthday, and is quietly furious most of the week. A good-person checklist can stop at two lines: don't do harm, do good.

Magha Puja remembers a verse with three. Theravada tradition tells of a full moon at the Bamboo Grove, monks arriving from all over without being called, and the Buddha giving them a few short verses to carry.

One of them is the verse a monk in a tree gave a poet a week ago, in Max Müller's translation: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened."
That day was about how hard it is to live. Today is about the third line, the one that gets skipped.

teach.b: So why is the mind on a list about conduct? In Pali the third line is sacittapariyodapanam: making your own mind clear. Not someone else's.
Your own. The answer is in how the Buddha understood action.
In the Anguttara Nikaya he says it plainly, in paraphrase: intention is what I call kamma; having intended, one acts, by body, by speech, by mind.
Read that way, the first two lines are the fruit, and the third is the root. A kind deed done from a furious mind still carries the fury somewhere. That's the heart of it.
So what does a clear mind look like?
The Anguttara Nikaya has a short pair of lines, in paraphrase: this mind is luminous, and it is stained by defilements that arrive from outside, like visitors.
Someone untaught doesn't see that, so the mind goes untrained; someone taught sees it, and trains. Notice the picture. The mind isn't rotten and in need of replacing.
It's bright, with guests tracking mud through it: the fury, the craving, the grudge. In that picture, cleaning means noticing the guests, not hating the house.
And it's your own house, which is why the third line says your own mind. A mind made clear isn't a new mind. It's the old one, with the mud gone.
On this full moon, people walk it out: at temples in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, they circle the temple at night with flowers, incense and a candle.

how: On the Magha full moon, Buddhists in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia go to the temple, hear a sermon, keep the precepts, and at night walk around the temple holding flowers, incense and a lit candle.

o: a day of fasting in memory of the Buddha's death
the full moon of the gathering and its three-line verse
the full moon that marks the start of the rains

games.q: three lines and a bright mind — tap the pairs.
p: the full moon of the gathering

s: the Magha Puja verse is all about good deeds
it has three lines, and the third, making your own mind clear, is the root of the other two.
the Buddha said intention is what he calls kamma
having intended, one acts, by body, speech and mind.
in the Anguttara picture, the mind itself is rotten
it calls the mind luminous, stained by defilements that arrive like visitors.

games.q: your friend helps everyone at the food bank but snaps at her sister all week. by the Magha Puja verse, what's missing?
o: the third line: clearing her own mind, where the deeds start.
nothing; doing good is the whole of the teaching.
more good deeds, enough to outweigh the snapping.
games.why: the verse has three lines, and the Buddha calls intention itself kamma. the deeds grow out of the mind.

practice: Stand, if you can, and walk one slow circle around your chair or your room, the way people circle the temple on this full moon. Give each stretch a line: not harming, doing good, and on the last stretch, letting the mind settle.
Then sit down where you started, and stay with that third line.

wordCard.voice: Magha Puja: the full moon of the gathering, and three lines: avoid evil, do good, purify your own mind.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: honoring on the full moon of the month of Magha.

carryVoice: Keep this one: the heart of it is the third line, a mind made clear. Seven of seven; the festival year is done.

sources.q: Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.63 (Nibbedhika Sutta: intention is kamma)
Anguttara Nikaya 1.51–52 (the luminous mind, stained by incoming defilements; the taught and untaught)
